title: NIST Project Aims to Accelerate Mobile Driver’s License Adoption
sourceName: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/11/nist-project-aims-accelerate-mobile-drivers-license-adoption A new form of digital identification called a mobile driver’s license (mDL) is making its way into American pockets — the ones that hold cellphones. An mDL offers a more secure and user-friendly experience than a physical identification card. A new draft report from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to make mDLs more widely usable for license holders and organizations alike. Twenty-two U.S. states and territories currently have active mDL programs. Across these programs, at least 5 million mDLs are in use around the U.S., with approximately 47% of the population having access to them. An mDL can be used either in person or online. It can potentially make many digital transactions easier: An individual could use one to open a bank account online or access government benefits. Its information is cryptographically protected, making it difficult to steal or fake. An mDL eliminates the need to upload photos of a physical ID card while also providing strong security because of the cryptographic information it contains. Despite these benefits, very few online service providers currently accept mDLs. “It’s a chicken-and-egg problem,” said NIST security engineer Bill Fisher. “On the one hand, consumers are unlikely to adopt mDLs unless they are accepted in high-value, everyday use cases. Meanwhile, companies are hesitant to invest in mDL integration without widespread consumer demand or adoption.” This issue helped motivate a project on mDLs from NIST’s National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence ( NCCoE ). The project’s draft report, entitled Digital Identities — Mobile Driver’s License (mDL): Enabling Secure and Interoperable Online Use (NIST Special Publication 1800-42) , offers tools and resources to help organizations assess the feasibility of integrating mDLs with their current systems. “Our goal is to help overcome the barriers preventing organizations from accepting mDLs online,” said Fisher, one of the project’s organizers. “By working with industry to test real-world applications, we can identify what’s working, what barriers remain, and provide a path to update their infrastructure so they can accommodate mDLs at a large scale.” The NCCoE project brought together stakeholders from across the mDL ecosystem , including technology companies, government agencies and five of the 10 largest U.S. banks, to identify emerging approaches to mDL adoption. The project created a reference architecture that demonstrates three capabilities: how users can present their mDLs when verifying their identity for an online transaction; how in certain high-risk scenarios — such as high-dollar transactions or account recovery — an mDL could be requested and presented to reestablish trust in the user’s identity; and how to issue a phishing-resistant authenticator (i.e., a passkey) to a user. “We built the system using commercially available, off-the-shelf technology, software and standards,” Fisher said. “We wanted to demonstrate how organizations can implement mDLs now, with minimum difficulty.” The draft report details the reference architecture and its components, then outlines how organizations and their customers can benefit from the improved security capabilities and privacy protections that mDLs offer. The report also outlines potential threats to an mDL ecosystem and risk mitigations, offering references to other NIST publications that can help maintain security, including the NIST Privacy Framework and the security and privacy control catalog ( NIST Special Publication 800-53 rev. 5 ). Additionally, the report offers recommendations on improving the user experience of mDL holders, including a set of seven best practices that reflect patterns observed during usability testing performed with a set of volunteers covering the system’s performance, satisfaction and feedback. Fisher said that while financial institutions provided the initial demonstration use case, the report contains information useful to any organization that accepts physical IDs now and is seeking to accept the presentation of mDLs. Other situations of broader applicability it addresses include accessing healthcare information and interacting with state and federal government services. “This is the direction technology is moving,” Fisher said. “But what limits current mDL adoption isn’t the technology itself, but the maturity of the surrounding ecosystem.
